newsitem.title: USA: Westell sees price cut on its Internet link.
newsitem.headline: Westell sees price cut on its Internet link.

text.p: Westell Technologies Inc said Thursday a faster, cheaper version of its Internet connection technology will be available in late 1996, which could reduce the cost of high-speed Internet access to $30 to $50 a month.
Westell chief executive Gary Seamans said the next generation of DSL (digital subscriber line) allows the enhanced connection to be set up for about $1,000.
"When the DSL system is down to $1,000 per home served, at that point (Internet service providers) can price the service at $30 to $50 a month and make a very nice profit," he said.
Seamans said $30 to $50 is the target price range for the home-user market. "We see our system there by the end of the calendar year."
Although Westell's other communications products accounted for about 75 percent of revenues in its last fiscal year, it sees DSL as its key opportunity.

Seamans said the company spent 40 percent of revenues on research and development, sales and marketing for the fiscal first quarter ended June 30. It said 75 percent of R and D goes to DSL technology.
Just a one percent market share of applying the technology to telephone lines world wide would mean $4 billion in revenues, Seamans said.
"Obviously that's a huge, huge opportunity for us," he said.

Westell now offers ADSL (asymmetric digital subscriber line) products which cost about $2,500 per line to set up but offer Internet connection about 50 times faster than the popular 28.8 kilobit per second modem. A Chicago-based Internet service provider, for example, currently shares set up costs with users and charges a $200 a month usage fee.
The technology runs on typical copper telephone lines with a box connected to a computer and another at a central hub.

With the new version, Seamans said the "Cable TV" model of supplying the box for free and charging a monthly service fee is feasible. At this point, some home users have indicated the initial investment is too pricey to make ADSL an option.

The DSL technology competes with cable modems which provide high-speed Internet access through cable TV hook ups. Various cable providers have begun testing and offering an Internet service, but Seamans said he is not threatened.
"The telephone companies in my view do not have a single possible way to compete against cable modems other than with ADSL data dialtone," Seamans said.

Other competition, however, sent Westell's stock price falling this week. Alcatel Telecom said it received an order for ADSL modems from a consortium of four telecommunications companies, and industry sources valued the deal at $300 million.
"I do not believe their outlook has changed," Kevin Slocum, an analyst for Soundview Financial Group said . "I believe there is plenty of opportunity out there."
